 Can Ossoff Help Elect a Black Woman Governor of Georgia?
 By 
 Ed Kilgore ,
 political columnist for Intelligencer since 2015 
 Oct. 20, 2026 
 Save this article to read it later.
 Find this story in your account’s ‘Saved for Later’ section.
 Photo: Pool/Atlanta News First 
 One of the most inspiring Democratic political stories of the 2026 midterm elections is the likely success of freshman U.S. senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia. In a state Donald Trump carried by more than 3 percent two years ago, Ossoff, a relatively progressive Jewish Democrat from Atlanta, looks to be running away with a reelection win over MAGA Congressman Mike Collins . He’s also making himself (willingly or not, since he denies any interest in a 2028 race) a dark-horse prospect for the presidency thanks to his viral fiery attacks on Trump and the GOP for systemic corruption . And it’s possible his popularity could help deliver another historic feat in Georgia.
 Ossoff, who was widely expected to be a prime GOP target this year, has instead built so strong a lead over Collins that Republicans appear to have decided against throwing good money after bad by committing the resources their candidate would need to catch up with the incumbent in spending or in the polls. Silver Bulletin’s polling averages show Ossoff leading Collins by 9.1 percent. But Republicans have a better chance for victory in Georgia’s other marquee statewide race. With two-term GOP governor Brian Kemp facing term limits, his party’s nomination went to previously little-known health-care tycoon Rick Jackson, who spent over $100 million of his personal fortune to make and then win a runoff over Trump endorsee and Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones after a campaign featuring extensive mutual mudslinging. With grudging if general GOP support (which is fine by Jackson, who is running as a poor-boy-who-made-good “outsider” candidate), Jackson has now unleashed another personally financed ad blitz on Democratic nominee and former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms . And he’s outspending Bottoms by an estimated 7-to-1 margin.
 The contest is reminding a lot of observers of the last two Georgia gubernatorial contests between Kemp and Democratic voter-mobilization wizard Stacey Abrams . In 2018, Abrams came tantalizingly close to breaking a GOP gubernatorial winning streak dating back to 1998. But in a 2022 rematch, Kemp won by a 53 percent–to–46 percent margin (and this was after he easily dispatched a Trump-backed rival in the primary). It was easy to mark up both Abrams losses to the reluctance of white Georgia voters to elect a Black woman to the position. But the racial interpretation of the 2022 vote was complicated by the concurrent Senate reelection of Ossoff’s Black colleague Raphael Warnock , and complicated even more by the fact that Warnock’s opponent was Black football legend and Trump crony Herschel Walker , whose personal problems caught up with him in a big way.
 Bottoms does not have Abrams’s iconic status in Georgia Democratic politics, but she was universally regarded as a national rising star when she was elected Atlanta’s mayor in 2017; she even made the short list of candidates to become Joe Biden ’s 2020 running mate. But her one term as mayor was marred by the same racial tensions and rising violent-crime rates that beset many cities during the COVID pandemic, and she lost the chance for a smoother second term (which she would have definitely won) by retiring and taking a sub-Cabinet job in Biden’s White House.
 Still, Bottoms solidified a comeback bid earlier this year by beating a large field to win the gubernatorial nomination without a runoff, even as Republicans battled and bickered, and she led Jackson in scattered early polls. Then came the inevitable barrage of negative ads from Jackson, some blasting Bottoms for “abandoning” Atlanta to go to Washington and others exploiting an incident from her tenure wherein anti-police protesters burned down a Wendy’s restaurant and a child was murdered in the subsequent violence. Clearly Republicans are also hoping that Bottoms’s close association with Atlanta city government will hurt her and Democrats generally in the rest of the state (and also in Atlanta’s suburbs), where fear and resentment of the megacity is chronic.
 Thanks to his largely unopposed advertising, Jackson now leads Bottoms narrowly in recent polls. A new survey from the Atlanta Journal-Constitution shows Jackson up among likely voters by one point (46 percent to 45 percent), with the billionaire achieving some success in describing himself as more of a protégé of the very popular Kemp than the unpopular Trump. So unsurprisingly, the big question has become whether the high-riding Ossoff can loan some support and money to his hard-pressed ticket mate. He’s certainly making an effort. In September he transferred $3.6 million to a coordinated campaign account backing the Democratic ticket (and there could be more of that if Republicans continue to abandon Collins), and he has been barnstorming with Bottoms . Next week former president Barack Obama will give both Democrats a lift at an Atlanta campaign rally.
 There’s a lot at stake for Ossoff in Bottoms’s success. If Jackson wins, Democrats may be cool to any Ossoff ’28 talk on grounds that his Senate seat is too precious to risk on a presidential run. Such an outcome could also feed concerns that other candidates (possibly even Warnock, who has recently spent some time in early 2028 primary states ) could do a better job of mobilizing the southern Black voters needed to take back the White House two years from now.
 Conversely, if Bottoms wins with a notable assist from Ossoff, it will represent a major racial and gender breakthrough in Georgia politics for which he will receive significant credit. Abrams was the first woman (Republican Karen Handel came very close in 2010, before going on to defeat none other than Jon Ossoff to win a congressional seat in 2017), and the first Black pol, to win a major-party gubernatorial nomination in Georgia; Bottoms is the second. If she can overcome Jackson’s bankroll, a biracial blue sweep would firmly reestablish Georgia as a purple state and potentially the southern foundation for a winning presidential coalition in 2028 and beyond. And if Ossoff does choose to run for president in 2028 or later (he’s only 39), he’d likely have an ally in a Governor Keisha Lance Bottoms.
